newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila says Spratlys hut dismantled.
newsitem.headline: Manila says Spratlys hut dismantled.

text.p: A hut-like structure sighted along with Chinese naval ships near islands claimed by Manila in the disputed Spratlys has been removed, a senior Philipine military officer said on Friday.

Major-General Reynaldo Reyes told reporters who flew over parts of the contested islands that Philippine Air Force planes first spotted the structure on April 25 but it had disappeared when the planes returned after a week.

Manila protested on April 30 against the presence of what it said were four armed Chinese vessels near Kota and Panata islands, two of the eight islands it claims in the Spratlys, a cluster of potentially oil-rich isles, reefs and shoals in the South China Sea.
The Philippine military also reported sighting several Chinese fishing boats and the hut-like structure near the two islands.
Beijing says the entire area historically belongs to China. The islands are also claimed wholly or in part by Vietnam, Taiwan, the Philippines, Malaysia and Brunei.
The Chinese embassy in Manila said the ships Manila had sighted were on a scientific research mission but they were withdrawn after the Philippines protested.
"...The structures that are supposed to be there are not there anymore," said Reyes, chief of the Western Command in charge of the Philippine-claimed islands.
Despite the withdrawal of the Chinese ships, Philippine reconnaissance aircraft continue to fly over the islands claimed by the Philippines, Reyes said.
He said that a day before the hut was spotted, Philippine soldiers on the islands "observed, heard sounds of machineries, especially during night time."
"During (those) times, ships had bright lights on, conducting unknown activities," he added.
The media team on a C-130 military plane flew twice over some of the islands claimed by Manila, accompanied by congressman Roque Ablan, chairman of the House of Representatives committee on defence.
The group later landed on Pagasa, the biggest of the eight Manila-claimed islands, where Ablan interviewed Filipino soldiers.
President Fidel Ramos, in a speech in Los Angeles on Wednesday during a visit to the United States, said there was a danger of the Spratlys becoming a flashpoint.

"For the Philipines, it is the Spratly Islands that is the nearest source of possible conflict ... Frankly, it is also for us the litmus test of whether China - as a great power - intends to play by international rules or makes its own."
